titulo: Amy Carmichael · The mother of Dohnavur

guion.texto: Dohnavur, at the southern tip of India, January 1951. Under a tree there is a grave with no headstone. She had asked that no stone be put on it. The children placed a birdbath on top with a single word: “Amma,” which in Tamil means “mother.” That is what hundreds of children she had rescued called her. Her story began far away, in a village by the Irish Sea.
Amy Beatrice Carmichael was born on December 16, 1867, in Millisle, a village on the coast of County Down, in Ireland.
She was the eldest of seven children. Her father, David, was a miller, and the family attended the village Presbyterian church.
As a teenager she studied at a girls’ boarding school in Harrogate, England.
There, at 15, during a special mission for children, she gave her life to Christ while a children’s hymn was being sung.
When she was 16, the family moved to Belfast. They attended the Rosemary Street Presbyterian Church.
In 1885 her father died. Amy had to leave school, and the family went through hard times.
One rainy Sunday, on the way home from church, Amy and two of her brothers saw a poor old woman carrying a heavy bundle, and they helped her.
They walked past “the respectable people,” who stared at them. Amy felt ashamed.
Beside a newly built fountain, some words from the Bible came to her mind:
“If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw, his workmanship will be evident.” (1 Corinthians 3:12-13 · BSB)
She told no one. But from that day, she later said, only eternal things mattered to her.
In Belfast there were thousands of girls who worked in the linen mills. They were called “shawlies,” because they could not afford a hat and covered their heads with a shawl.
Amy started a Sunday morning class for them. At first there were only a few; in time there were several hundred.
She also worked among the poor in the slums of Belfast, teaching children and visiting homes.
There was no longer room in the church hall. Amy saw an advertisement in a magazine for an iron hall that held five hundred people and cost five hundred pounds.
A woman, Kate Mitchell, gave the money, and a mill owner donated the land.
In January 1889 the Welcome Hall opened, on the corner of Cambrai Street. A church is still there today: the Welcome Evangelical Church.
In 1887 she heard Hudson Taylor preach, the founder of the China Inland Mission. That year she met Robert Wilson, a 62-year-old Quaker industrialist.
Wilson was one of the founders of the Keswick Convention, a large yearly gathering of Christians by the lakes of northern England.
He welcomed her into his home like a daughter, though he never adopted her legally. Amy called him “Fatherie” and began to sign her name “Amy Wilson-Carmichael.”
In 1892, at Wilson’s home, she felt that God was telling her: “Go.”
She applied to the China Inland Mission, but they turned her down because of her health.
Robert Wilson wrote her a sentence that she kept in her Bible:
Follow no voice, not mine or any other which is not His.
On March 3, 1893, she sailed for the East on the steamer Valetta. She was the first missionary sent out by the Keswick Convention.
She wrote her first letter while the harbor pilot was still on board. It began:
Our Saviour has two nail-pierced hands…
Robert Wilson wrote to her every week from that day on.
In May 1893 she reached Matsue, a city in Japan beside a lake, to work with the missionary Barclay Buxton. The church was a former Shinto temple.
She persuaded the other missionaries to wear kimonos, like the local women.
In July 1894 she fell ill and had to leave. She thought it would be only for a few weeks. She wrote:
One might be going away for six years instead of six weeks. I never knew I loved them so dearly.
She went by way of Ceylon and returned to England: Robert Wilson had suffered a stroke.
In 1895 a women’s missionary society of the Church of England accepted her, even though she was not an Anglican. In November she reached South India, sick with dengue fever.
She never went home again. She stayed in India for fifty-five years.
She learned Tamil and began to preach in the villages of the Tinnevelly district with the missionary Thomas Walker and his wife.
In 1897 Ponnammal, a young Christian widow, joined her. Then other Tamil women and girls came.

They traveled at night in bullock carts, to avoid the heat, and preached from village to village. They carried a satin banner of black, red, white and yellow, and used its colors to explain the gospel.
The people called us by a name meaning a constellation like Orion or the Pleiades.
At the end of 1898, a newly baptized man said to his wife:
“Give me your jewels. What does a winner of souls want with jewels?” (Quoted by Amy Carmichael · BSB)
From then on, the women of the band stopped wearing jewelry.
Preena was seven years old. Her father had died, and some women from a Hindu temple wanted to raise her to be “married to the god.”
She had already run away once and walked to her mother’s house in Tuticorin. But the temple women followed her, and her mother, afraid of the gods, gave her back.
On the night of March 6, 1901, she slipped out of the temple again without anyone stopping her. She crossed a stream and a palm grove.
A kind woman took her in that night and in the morning brought her to the missionary.
The next day, Preena told her what her life had been like in the temple house. Amy wrote:
When first we heard from the lips of a little child the story of her life in a Temple house, we were startled and distressed.
That is how she learned that many girls were given to the temples for a life of abuse. From then on she gave her life to rescuing them.
Preena stayed with her. They called her “the Elf.”
In 1902 they settled in Dohnavur, a dry, sunburnt place at the foot of the mountains. There was an old mud bungalow that was falling apart and a yard full of goats.
They did not expect to stay more than a year.
The first nursery was a single room with a mud floor: nursery, kitchen and bedroom all at once. Amy never asked anyone for money; she asked only God, and the money came.
A pastor traveled more than a hundred miles to bring them a baby girl rescued from the house of a temple woman. She was the first temple baby to come to Dohnavur.
Preena chose her name while reading Revelation:
“…the eleventh jacinth, and the twelfth amethyst.” (Revelation 21:20 · BSB)
So our first Temple baby is called Amethyst.
Amethyst died soon after. Many of the first babies died, and for a time Ponnammal took the others to be cared for near a mission hospital.
In 1903 she published a book in London about what she had seen: “Things as They Are.”

In England many did not believe her. For the fourth edition she added notes from other missionaries confirming what she said. An English official who thought the book was lying investigated, and ended up agreeing with her.
We shall have all eternity to celebrate the victories, but we have only the few hours before sunset in which to win them.
On August 24, 1912, Thomas Walker died. His wife, ill in England, answered with a telegram:
“The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD.” (Job 1:21 · BSB)
Three years later, on August 26, 1915, Ponnammal, the first companion of the band, died of cancer.
By 1913 about a hundred and thirty girls lived in Dohnavur. In 1918 Amy began to take in boys as well: unprotected boys faced the same dangers.
That September, the children climbed the mountain river looking for its source. From then on, groups went up every year to a house in the mountains.
In 1925 they left their mission societies to go on by faith alone. In 1927 they registered the work as the Dohnavur Fellowship. Its charter named an “Unseen Leader” as its head: Christ.
In 1921 they had prayed for a hospital: the nearest one was two days away. In 1928 they bought the land, and in 1929 a gift of a thousand pounds arrived.
They named it Parama Suha Salai: “Place of Heavenly Healing.” It would be above all a hospital for children.
In 1931, at 63, she fell into a pit at a building site and broke her leg.
From then on she spent almost twenty years in her room, nearly always in bed.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9 · BSB)
From her bed she went on leading the work, trained those who would carry it on, Indian and European, and wrote many of her books: about 35 in all.
The children called her “Amma.” In one of her books she wrote:
If I have not compassion on my fellow-servant, even as my Lord had pity on me, then I know nothing of Calvary’s love.
Amy Carmichael died in Dohnavur on January 18, 1951. She was 83. She had lived in India for fifty-five years without ever going home.

In the late 1940s, a law in Madras banned the dedication of girls to the temples. Today the Dohnavur Fellowship is still in the same place, led by Indian Christians. It has a children’s home, a hospital and schools, and it is carried on by people who grew up there.
“In the same way, your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should perish.” (Matthew 18:14 · BSB)

Sources: Amy Carmichael’s books (From Sunrise Land, Things as They Are, Overweights of Joy, Lotus Buds, Walker of Tinnevelly, Ponnamal and Gold Cord), the Presbyterian Historical Society of Ireland, the EPIC museum in Dublin, Christian History, the Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions and the Dohnavur Fellowship. Amy’s words are quotations from her books. The first girl is called Preena in her 1909 book; in 1932 she called her Pearleyes.
